# Alert Handler Behavioral Specification

## 1. Scope

This specification defines the behavior of the alert handler module. The alert handler is a bus-accessible security peripheral that:

- Receives alert events from alert sources.
- Classifies those events into one of four alert classes.
- Raises a class interrupt for software.
- If software does not handle the interrupt, optionally escalates by driving escalation outputs.
- Continuously checks the health of alert and escalation signaling paths using ping testing.
- Provides low-power handling so that alert channels in clock-gated or reset domains do not produce false alarms.
- Exposes a crashdump snapshot for hardware debug and security state capture.

The number of alert channels is a configuration-time parameter. The behavior described here applies uniformly to every configured alert channel.

## 2. General Device Behavior

### 2.1 Reset State

After reset, the module must enter a quiescent state:

- All class interrupt outputs must be deasserted.
- All escalation outputs must be inactive.
- The ping mechanism must be disabled.
- All alert channels must be disabled until configured by software.
- The crashdump output and all other observable outputs must be at defined reset values.

No alert, interrupt, escalation, or ping-failure activity may be reported solely due to reset assertion or deassertion.

### 2.2 Configuration Interface

The module must implement a memory-mapped register interface. Software must be able to:

- Enable or disable each external and local alert.
- Assign each enabled alert to one of four classes.
- Lock configuration registers to prevent further modification.
- Program ping timeout and ping enable settings.
- Program per-class accumulation thresholds, interrupt timeout values, escalation phase durations, escalation output enables, and phase-to-escalation mappings.
- Read status, cause, counter, and state information.
- Clear interrupts, cause bits, accumulation counters, and escalation state when permitted.

The module must ignore writes to locked configuration registers. Locked registers must remain locked until the next reset.

Critical configuration registers must be protected so that storage or update errors can be detected. If such an error is detected, the module must report it as a local alert event, and the affected configuration must not be treated as trustworthy.

## 3. Alert Event Processing

### 3.1 Alert Inputs

The module must provide one alert channel for each configured alert source. Each channel uses differential signaling.

For each alert channel, the module must:

- Detect an incoming alert event.
- Respond with the required acknowledgement sequence on the alert channel.
- Record the event for classification.
- Continue to acknowledge repeated alert events while the source continues to assert the event.

The module must support both synchronous and asynchronous alert channel operation. For asynchronous channels, the module must ensure that a valid alert event is not lost when crossing clock domains.

### 3.2 Signal Integrity Monitoring

Each alert channel must be continuously monitored for differential signal integrity failures. The module must report a signal integrity failure for that channel when:

- The incoming differential signal encoding is invalid.
- The remote side explicitly signals an integrity failure through a defined invalid signaling pattern.

A signal integrity failure on an alert channel must not be treated as a valid alert event.

For disabled alert channels, signal integrity failure reporting must not cause a local alert.

### 3.3 Disabled Alert Behavior

An alert that is disabled by software must not:

- Set an alert cause bit.
- Trigger a class interrupt.
- Increment an accumulation counter.
- Trigger escalation.

## 4. Classification and Interrupt Generation

### 4.1 Classification

Each external alert and each local alert must have an enable bit and a class assignment. When enabled, each alert must be assigned to exactly one of four classes: A, B, C, or D.

When an enabled alert event is received, the module must set the corresponding sticky cause bit for that alert. The cause bit remains set until software clears it, even if the original alert source deasserts.

Local alert events must be handled through the same classification path as external alerts.

### 4.2 Class Interrupts

The module must provide one interrupt output per class.

Whenever any enabled alert assigned to a class triggers, the module must assert that class interrupt.

The interrupt must remain asserted until software clears the corresponding class interrupt state. Clearing the interrupt state must not clear alert cause bits.

Software test writes to interrupt test registers must assert the corresponding class interrupt, but must not increment accumulation counters and must not set alert cause bits.

### 4.3 Simultaneous Alerts

If multiple alert events assigned to the same class arrive in the same cycle, the module must:

- Set the sticky cause bit for every one of those alerts.
- Assert the class interrupt.
- Increment the class accumulation counter by one, not by the number of simultaneous events.

## 5. Accumulation and Escalation Triggers

### 5.1 Accumulation Counter

Each class must have an accumulation counter.

The accumulation counter must increment for each class trigger event. If the configured accumulation threshold is N, then escalation is triggered on the (N+1)th class trigger event. A threshold of 0 means the first class trigger event immediately triggers escalation.

The accumulation counter must saturate at its maximum value and must not wrap.

Software must be able to clear the accumulation counter unless clearing is locked. If clearing is locked, the clear operation must have no effect.

Clearing the accumulation counter while escalation is active must abort the escalation protocol and return the class to idle, unless the class is locked against clearing.

### 5.2 Interrupt Timeout

Each class must support an interrupt timeout value.

The interrupt timeout runs while the corresponding class interrupt is asserted. If the timeout value is zero, the timeout mechanism is disabled.

If the class interrupt remains asserted longer than the configured timeout, the module must trigger that class’s escalation protocol.

Clearing the class interrupt before timeout must stop and reset the timeout counter.

### 5.3 Class Enable

If a class is disabled, it must not generate interrupts, accumulation, or escalation.

If a class has all escalation output enables cleared, the class escalation protocol must be effectively disabled.

## 6. Escalation Protocol

### 6.1 Escalation Phases

When a class escalation trigger occurs, the module must start the class escalation protocol.

The escalation protocol must advance through up to four phases in fixed order: phase 0, phase 1, phase 2, phase 3.

Each phase must have a programmable duration. Each phase must last at least one clock cycle, even if the programmed value is zero.

After phase 3 completes, the class must remain in a terminal escalation state until cleared or reset.

### 6.2 Escalation Outputs

The module must provide four escalation severity outputs.

During each escalation phase, the module must assert the escalation outputs that are enabled and mapped to that phase.

The mapping of phases to escalation outputs must be software-configurable per class.

Software must be able to read the current escalation state and the current escalation counter for each class.

### 6.3 Clearing Escalation

Unless locked, software must be able to clear an active escalation protocol by writing the class clear register.

If the class is locked against clearing, once escalation begins, it must not be stopped by software until reset.

### 6.4 Escalation Signaling Behavior

Escalation signaling must use differential signaling with response monitoring.

The module must:

- Encode a true escalation request as a differential pulse longer than one cycle.
- Encode a ping request as a single-cycle differential pulse.
- Monitor the incoming response signaling for the required response pattern.
- Report a signal integrity failure if the escalation response is missing or malformed.

If an escalation signaling integrity failure is detected on any escalation channel, the module must generate an escalation signal integrity local alert.

## 7. Ping Testing

### 7.1 Ping Operation

The module must implement a ping mechanism that periodically tests alert and escalation signaling paths.

The ping mechanism must be disabled by default and must only operate after software enables it.

Only alert channels that are both enabled and locked must be pinged. Escalation channels, once the ping mechanism is enabled, must always be pinged.

The ping interval and, for alert channels, the ping target must be randomized. Ping timing must not be predictable from software-visible state.

The module must obtain entropy from its entropy interface and use it to randomize ping timing and alert-channel selection.

The module must enforce a minimum spacing between ping operations.

### 7.2 Escalation Ping Ordering

Escalation channels must be pinged in a bounded, in-order sequence. This is required so that remote liveness monitors can depend on a maximum gap between escalation pings.

### 7.3 Ping Responses

When a ping is sent, the module must wait for a valid ping response.

If the ping response is received before the configured ping timeout, the ping operation must complete normally.

If the ping response is not received before the configured ping timeout, the module must generate a ping failure local alert:

- For alert channels: alert ping failure.
- For escalation channels: escalation ping failure.

If a ping response is received when no ping was requested, the module must treat that as a ping failure and generate the corresponding local alert.

### 7.4 Ping Timer Integrity

The module must detect internal integrity errors in the ping generation logic.

If an internal ping-generation integrity error is detected, the module must assert both the alert ping-failure and escalation ping-failure local alerts continuously until reset.

## 8. Local Alert Sources

The module must generate the following local alert events:

- Alert channel ping failure.
- Escalation channel ping failure.
- Alert channel signal integrity failure, only for enabled alert channels.
- Escalation channel signal integrity failure.
- Configuration bus integrity failure.
- Shadow configuration register update error.
- Shadow configuration register storage error.

Each local alert event must be recorded in a local alert cause register and must be classifiable and enablable in the same manner as external alert events.

## 9. Low-Power Behavior

### 9.1 Low-Power Indications

The module receives low-power indication inputs indicating, for each low-power group, whether the associated alert sources are clock-gated or held in reset.

These indications must be treated as multibit encoded signals. The module must use them to determine which alert channels are in a low-power state.

### 9.2 Behavior While Low-Power

While an alert channel is in a low-power state, the module must:

- Not report alert events from that channel.
- Not report ping failures for that channel.
- Suppress spurious events that may occur as a result of the remote side being reset or clock-gated.

The module must ensure that ping requests to low-power alert channels are handled in a way that does not cause false ping-failure local alerts.

### 9.3 Recovery After Low-Power

When a low-power condition deasserts, the module must reinitialize the affected alert channel so that it returns to a known operating state.

If the affected alert source was reset while the module was not reset, the alert channel must be brought back to a coherent state before normal alert and ping operation resumes.

If reinitialization does not complete successfully, the ping mechanism must eventually detect the channel as faulty and report a ping failure.

### 9.4 Module Reset While Remote Sources Remain Powered

If the module itself is reset while some alert sources remain active, the module must reinitialize all affected alert channels after reset release. This must prevent stale or inconsistent channel state from producing false alerts or ping failures.

## 10. Entropy Interface

The module must request entropy from the entropy distribution network to reseed its ping randomization logic.

The entropy request and response behavior must follow the defined entropy interface protocol.

The module must not require software intervention to request or consume entropy after initialization.

## 11. Crashdump Output

The module must provide a crashdump output that contains:

- The current sticky alert cause bits.
- The current local alert cause bits.
- The current accumulation counter value for each class.
- The current escalation counter value for each class.
- The current escalation state for each class.

The crashdump output must be continuously updated with live state until the crashdump latch condition occurs.

The crashdump latch condition occurs when any class reaches the escalation phase configured as the crashdump trigger phase for that class.

After the first latch condition occurs, the module must hold the crashdump output constant until reset or until all classes that requested capture have been cleared. While it is held, subsequent state changes must not alter the latched crashdump output.

## 12. Internal Integrity Failure Behavior

### 12.1 Class Accumulation and Escalation Integrity

The module must detect integrity errors in class accumulation and escalation timing logic.

If such an integrity error is detected in any class, the module must:

- Assert all escalation severity outputs.
- Place the affected class in a terminal error state.
- Remain in that state until reset.

### 12.2 Register and Bus Integrity

The module must detect integrity failures on its configuration bus interface and in shadowed configuration storage.

If a bus integrity failure is detected, the module must report it as a local alert.

If a shadow register update or storage error is detected, the module must report it as a local alert.

## 13. Bus Interface Behavior

The module must implement all register accesses with standard bus handshaking.

All reads and writes to valid registers must complete without hanging the bus.

Writes to locked, reserved, or unimplemented registers must not change module state. The module must respond to such accesses according to the bus protocol.

The module must allow software to read:

- Alert cause and local alert cause registers.
- Class accumulation counters.
- Class escalation counters.
- Class escalation states.
- Configuration and lock status.

The module must allow software to clear, when permitted:

- Alert cause bits.
- Local alert cause bits.
- Class interrupt state.
- Class accumulation counters.
- Class escalation state.

# Behavioral Design Specification: Alert Handler Register Wrapper

## 1. Scope

This module provides the software-visible register interface for the alert handler. It is a bus slave that:

- Exposes configuration and status registers.
- Generates one interrupt per alert class.
- Passes configuration information to the alert handler core.
- Captures hardware status into software-readable registers.
- Provides a crashdump snapshot output.
- Reports bus integrity and shadowed-register errors.

This module does not implement the alert classification, escalation, or ping protocol itself. It only provides the register-facing behavior, interrupt state handling, status mapping, and crashdump snapshot behavior described below.

## 2. Reset Behavior

On reset, the module must:

- Clear all internal state and register storage.
- Deassert all class interrupt outputs.
- Clear all crashdump latch state and any captured crashdump snapshot.
- Return all configuration outputs to their reset values.
- Deassert error status outputs that are not caused by a persistent error condition.

The module must support resetting shadowed register storage separately from the rest of the logic. The main reset clears all non-shadowed state, while the shadowed reset clears the shadowed register storage.

## 3. Bus Interface and Register Access

The module must behave as a slave on the TileLink-UL bus. It must:

- Accept incoming read and write transactions and return protocol-valid responses.
- Never initiate bus transactions on its own.
- Present registers according to the defined register map.
- Preserve the normal read/write semantics of control and status registers.
- Honor register write-enable and lock behavior.
- Honor shadowed-register update semantics.

Device mode for the register block is permanently enabled. Register access must not depend on an external debug-mode signal.

When a bus transaction fails integrity checking, the module must assert a dedicated fatal integrity alert output. This alert must be observable regardless of the state of other configuration registers.

Shadowed-register storage errors and shadowed-register update errors must be reported as separate status flags to the alert handler core. These flags are intended to be used as local alert sources.

## 4. Interrupt Generation

The module must provide four class interrupt outputs, one for each alert class.

For each class:

- The interrupt output must be asserted only when the corresponding interrupt state bit is set and the corresponding interrupt enable bit is set.
- The interrupt state bit must be set by a hardware event for that class.
- The interrupt state bit must also be set when software writes the corresponding interrupt test bit.
- Setting the state bit must not depend on the interrupt enable value.
- Software must be able to clear the interrupt state bit by writing to the interrupt state register.
- A test write must not set alert cause bits, increment class counters, or trigger escalation accumulation. It affects only the interrupt state.

## 5. Alert Cause Recording

The module must maintain sticky cause bits for every external alert source and every local alert source.

For each cause bit:

- The bit must be set when the corresponding hardware event is reported.
- If the bit is already set, a new event must keep it set.
- The bit must not be automatically cleared by hardware.
- Software must be able to clear the bit through the corresponding cause register.

The current value of each cause bit must also be included in the crashdump output.

## 6. Hardware Status Readback

The module must capture the following hardware status information and make it software-readable through the register interface:

- Current class accumulation counts.
- Current class escalation counts.
- Current class escalation state.

These values must be passed through without modification. They must also be available to the crashdump output.

## 7. Configuration Outputs to the Alert Handler Core

The module must provide configuration outputs derived from the programmed registers.

The module must provide:

- The ping timer enable value.
- The ping timeout value.
- Per-alert ping enable values.
- Per-alert enable and class assignment values.
- Per-local-alert enable and class assignment values.
- Per-class effective enable.
- Per-class escalation signal enable values.
- Per-class escalation phase mapping values.
- Per-class accumulator thresholds.
- Per-class interrupt timeout values.
- Per-class escalation phase duration values.
- Per-class crashdump trigger phase selection.
- Per-class clear pulses.

A per-alert ping enable must be asserted only when the alert is enabled and its configuration is locked. This ensures that only enabled and locked alert channels are pinged.

The per-class effective enable must be asserted only when the class master enable is set and at least one escalation signal enable for that class is set. If all escalation signal enables for a class are zero, the class must be treated as disabled.

## 8. Class Clear and Autolock Behavior

The module must generate a class-clear pulse when software writes 1 to an accepted class-clear register.

The module must also support automatic locking of class clearing:

- Each class has a clear write-enable register that controls whether software may clear that class state.
- If the class control lock bit is set, the class is enabled, and hardware indicates that escalation has been triggered for that class, the module must automatically clear the class clear write-enable.
- Once this automatic clear occurs, software must no longer be able to clear the class accumulation or escalation state through the class-clear register.

This behavior applies independently to each class.

## 9. Crashdump Snapshot Behavior

The crashdump output must expose a fixed collection of alert handler state information, including alert cause bits, local alert cause bits, class accumulation counts, class escalation counts, and class escalation state.

The output must operate as follows:

- Before any crashdump capture has occurred, the output must reflect the live current state.
- When a hardware crashdump latch trigger is asserted for any class, the module must capture the current crashdump state into a snapshot.
- If multiple class triggers assert in the same cycle, only one snapshot is captured.
- After a snapshot has been captured, the crashdump output must be held at the snapshot value.
- While a snapshot is held, new hardware trigger assertions must not overwrite it.
- The snapshot remains held until all classes that asserted a latch trigger have had their class state cleared by an accepted class-clear operation.
- When all such latch conditions are cleared, the crashdump output must return to live current state.
- After re-arming, a later trigger may capture a new snapshot.

This behavior prevents later escalation side effects from overwriting the original alert cause information.

## 10. Error Reporting

The module must provide the following error outputs:

- A fatal bus integrity alert, asserted when an incoming bus transaction fails integrity checking.
- A shadowed storage error flag, asserted when shadowed register storage fails.
- A shadowed update error flag, asserted when the shadowed-register update protocol is violated.

These error indicators must not be masked by normal register enable or lock settings. They are intended to be used by the alert handler as local alert sources.

# Alert Handler Behavioral Specification

## 1. Overview

The alert handler is a system peripheral that collects security-relevant alert events from multiple sources, records which sources caused them, assigns them to one of four handling classes, and raises the corresponding class interrupt. If software does not service the interrupt, the alert handler can start a programmable escalation sequence that drives one or more escalation outputs intended to trigger hardware countermeasures.

The module also continuously checks the health of the alert and escalation signaling paths. It does this by periodically issuing ping operations and by monitoring the integrity of the differential signaling used for alert and escalation messages. Any detected problem is reported as a local alert and processed through the same classification and escalation machinery as external alerts.

## 2. Behavioral Summary

- Receives one or more external alert events.
- Provides differential acknowledgement and ping signaling back to each alert source.
- Maintains sticky cause bits for every external and local alert source.
- Assigns each alert to one of four classes or disables it.
- Produces one interrupt output per class.
- Counts alerts per class and can trigger escalation when a threshold is exceeded.
- Can trigger escalation when a class interrupt remains unserviced for a programmable timeout.
- Drives four escalation outputs through a programmable sequence of phases.
- Monitors escalation response signaling and reports integrity failures.
- Periodically pings alert and escalation channels to verify that they are alive.
- Supports low-power groups by suppressing ping failures and ignoring events while an alert source is clock-gated or in reset.
- Provides a crashdump snapshot of alert causes and class state.
- Requests entropy periodically to maintain randomness in ping scheduling.

## 3. Interface-Related Behavior

### 3.1 Configuration Interface

The module is accessed as a bus peripheral. Software uses this interface to configure alert enables, class assignments, ping settings, class thresholds, escalation phase timing, and lock controls.

The module shall:

- Present read and write access to its configuration and status registers.
- Ignore writes to locked configuration registers.
- Assert a local bus-integrity alert if a bus transfer fails its integrity check.
- Keep all configuration in a safe, disabled state after reset.

### 3.2 Interrupt Outputs

The module provides four interrupt outputs, one for each alert class.

An interrupt output shall be asserted when the corresponding class interrupt status is set and the interrupt is enabled. The interrupt shall remain asserted until software clears the interrupt status.

Clearing a class interrupt status shall also stop any interrupt timeout associated with that class.

### 3.3 Alert Channels

Each external alert source is connected through a differential signaling interface. The module shall:

- Detect a valid alert event from an enabled source.
- Complete the required acknowledgement handshake so the alert source can deassert and later repeat the event.
- Treat the alert event as a single event for classification purposes, even if the source continues to hold or repeat the alert.
- Ignore alert events from disabled alert sources.
- Detect invalid differential encodings on the alert channel and report them as a local alert.

Alert channels may be asynchronous with respect to the module clock. The module shall correctly receive and acknowledge events regardless of the relative clock relationships.

### 3.4 Escalation Channels

The module provides four escalation outputs. Each escalation output uses differential signaling and has a corresponding response input from the escalation receiver.

The module shall:

- Drive the selected escalation output with a valid escalation message for the required duration.
- Monitor the response input while an escalation message is active.
- Report a local alert if the expected response is missing or invalid.
- Ping each escalation channel periodically and report a local alert if the response is not correct.

### 3.5 Low-Power Group Indications

The module receives multibit indications that groups of alert sources are either clock-gated or held in reset.

For any alert channel whose source is indicated to be in a low-power state, the module shall:

- Suppress ping failures for that channel while the low-power condition is active.
- Ignore alert events from that channel during the low-power condition.
- Treat pings to that channel as satisfied rather than reporting them as failures.
- Reinitialize the alert channel when the low-power condition is removed.

The low-power behavior shall not generate false interrupts or false local alerts.

### 3.6 Entropy Interface

The module uses an entropy interface to obtain fresh randomness for its ping scheduling.

The module shall:

- Issue entropy requests periodically.
- Incorporate the returned entropy into the ping scheduling process.
- Continue ping scheduling in a safe manner when entropy is not available.

### 3.7 Crashdump Output

The module provides a crashdump output that reflects a snapshot of selected internal state. This includes:

- Sticky cause bits for external alerts.
- Sticky cause bits for local alerts.
- The current accumulation count for each class.
- The current escalation counter for each class.
- The current escalation state for each class.

The crashdump output shall track live state until a crashdump latch condition occurs. Once latched, the output shall remain constant until the module is reset or every class that requested capture has been cleared.

## 4. Functional Requirements

### 4.1 Reset and Startup Behavior

After reset, the module shall be in a quiescent state:

- All external alerts and local alerts shall be disabled.
- No class interrupt shall be asserted.
- No escalation output shall be active.
- Ping operations shall not be started.
- No ping-failure or integrity-failure local alert shall be asserted.
- All shadowed configuration registers shall have matching reset values.
- The crashdump output shall be unlatched and follow the reset state.

### 4.2 Configuration and Locking

Software shall be able to configure the module before normal operation begins. The following settings shall be software-programmable:

- Enable or disable each external alert.
- Enable or disable each local alert.
- Assign each external or local alert to one of the four classes.
- Enable or disable pinging for eligible alert channels.
- Set the ping timeout value.
- Enable or disable the global ping mechanism.
- Enable or disable escalation for each class.
- Set the accumulation threshold for each class.
- Set the interrupt timeout for each class.
- Set the duration of each escalation phase.
- Select which escalation outputs are enabled and which phase drives each output.
- Select the class phase that latches the crashdump snapshot.

Each security-relevant configuration field shall be lockable. Once locked, writes to that field shall have no effect until the next reset.

Only alert channels that are both enabled and locked shall be eligible for pinging. Escalation channels shall be eligible for pinging whenever the global ping mechanism is enabled.

### 4.3 Alert Event Handling

An external alert event on an enabled and out-of-low-power channel shall:

1. Set the sticky cause bit for that alert source.
2. Be classified into the class assigned to that source.
3. Cause the class interrupt status for that class to be set.

An alert event on a disabled channel shall be ignored. It shall not set the cause bit, generate an interrupt, or affect class accumulation.

Local alerts shall be handled in the same way as external alerts. They shall have their own sticky cause bits, enable controls, class assignments, and lock controls.

Cause bits shall remain set until software clears them. Clearing a cause bit shall not itself clear a class interrupt or reset class accumulation.

### 4.4 Ping Testing

The module shall continuously schedule ping operations when the global ping mechanism is enabled.

Ping operations shall occur at pseudo-random intervals. The interval between pings shall be randomized so that ping timing is not easily predictable.

For alert channels, the ping scheduler shall only select channels that are enabled, locked, and not in a low-power state.

For escalation channels, all channels shall be pinged in a bounded manner. The scheduling shall guarantee that the interval between pings to the same escalation channel is bounded.

When a ping is issued:

- The module shall wait for a valid ping response.
- If the response arrives before the programmed ping timeout, the ping is considered successful.
- If the response does not arrive before the programmed timeout, the module shall assert the corresponding ping-failure local alert.
- If a ping response arrives when no ping was requested for that channel, the module shall assert a ping-failure local alert.

Pings to a channel in a low-power state shall not produce ping-failure alerts.

### 4.5 Classification and Class Interrupts

Each enabled alert is assigned to exactly one of four classes. When an enabled alert fires, the class interrupt status for its assigned class shall be set.

The interrupt output for a class shall be independent of whether escalation is enabled for that class. An alert assigned to a class shall raise the class interrupt even if the class escalation mechanism is disabled.

Software shall be able to clear each class interrupt status independently. Clearing the class interrupt status shall not clear alert cause bits and shall not reset the accumulation counter.

### 4.6 Escalation Triggers

Escalation for a class can be triggered by two mechanisms:

1. **Accumulation threshold**  
   Each new alert assigned to the class increments the class accumulation counter. The counter shall saturate rather than wrap. When the counter exceeds the programmed accumulation threshold, escalation shall be triggered.  
   If the threshold is zero, the first alert assigned to the class triggers escalation.

2. **Interrupt timeout**  
   If the class interrupt remains asserted for the programmed interrupt timeout, escalation shall be triggered.  
   An interrupt timeout of zero shall disable this mechanism.

When escalation has already been triggered, further triggers shall not restart the escalation sequence unless software clears the class first.

Software shall be able to clear the accumulation counter and abort an in-progress escalation sequence unless clearing has been disabled for that class. Clearing the class interrupt status shall not by itself clear the accumulation counter.

### 4.7 Escalation Protocol

Once escalation is triggered for a class, the class shall enter a programmable escalation sequence.

The escalation sequence shall consist of up to four phases, numbered zero through three. Phases shall execute in order.

Each phase shall have a programmable duration. If a phase duration is programmed to zero, the phase shall still last at least one cycle.

Each escalation output shall be independently enabled and assigned to one of the four phases. When the class enters the phase assigned to an enabled escalation output, that output shall be driven with an escalation message for the entire phase duration.

When the escalation sequence completes, the class shall enter a terminal escalation state. If software clearing is allowed, software may clear the class and return it to idle. If clearing is disabled, the terminal state shall persist until reset.

### 4.8 Local Alerts

The module shall generate local alerts for the following conditions:

- A ping to an alert channel failed.
- A ping to an escalation channel failed.
- A differential signal-integrity failure was detected on an alert channel.
- A differential signal-integrity failure was detected on an escalation channel.
- A bus transaction integrity failure was detected.
- A shadowed configuration register update failed.
- A shadowed configuration register storage mismatch was detected.

Each local alert shall be treated as an alert source. It may be enabled or disabled, assigned to a class, locked, and cleared by software.

Local alert cause bits shall be sticky. They shall remain set until software clears them.

### 4.9 Crashdump Latching

The crashdump output shall continuously reflect current state until it is latched.

A class shall have a configurable crashdump trigger phase. When a class enters that phase and the crashdump has not already been latched, the module shall latch the current crashdump snapshot.

After the crashdump output has been latched, it shall not change, even if subsequent alert events or escalation state changes occur.

The crashdump latch shall remain held until the module is reset or every class that requested capture has been cleared.

### 4.10 Fault and Glitch Robustness

The module shall detect illegal internal states in its hardened logic and respond in a deterministic manner.

If a fault is detected in the ping scheduling logic:

- The module shall stop issuing new ping operations.
- All ping-related local alerts shall be asserted.
- The state shall persist until reset.

If a fault is detected in a class accumulation or escalation timing logic:

- The module shall assert the escalation outputs.
- The affected class shall enter an error state.
- The error state and escalation output assertion shall persist until reset.

If a shadowed register storage mismatch or update failure is detected:

- The module shall assert the corresponding local alert.
- Writes to the affected register shall not be accepted as valid.

## 5. Operational Modes

### 5.1 Disabled Mode

After reset, before software configures the module, all alerts are disabled. The module shall not generate interrupts, escalation, or ping traffic.

### 5.2 Configured and Locked Mode

After software has enabled and locked the desired alerts and class configuration, normal operation begins. In this mode:

- Alert events are processed and classified.
- Class interrupts are generated.
- Ping operations run.
- Escalation can be triggered.

### 5.3 Low-Power Mode

When a low-power group indication is active, the affected alert channels are temporarily treated as unavailable. No ping failure or integrity failure shall be reported solely because the source is in low power. Normal processing resumes after the low-power indication is removed and the channel is reinitialized.

### 5.4 Escalation Active Mode

When a class is in its escalation sequence, further alert events in that class may continue to set cause bits and raise interrupts, but they shall not restart or alter the escalation sequence.

### 5.5 Terminal Error Mode

If software has locked the class against clearing, or if an internal fault is detected, the class can enter a terminal state that persists until reset. In this state, escalation behavior is deterministic and cannot be changed by software.

# Alert Handler Register Wrapper Specification

## 1. Purpose

This module provides the register, interrupt, status, and crashdump interface for the alert handler. It is responsible for exposing the software-visible configuration and status registers, generating the four class interrupts, translating hardware status into readable state, and providing a latched crashdump snapshot when escalation begins.

## 2. Bus and Register Access

- The module shall act as a bus slave on the TileLink-UL interface.
- It shall decode bus reads and writes within its assigned register address region according to the defined alert handler register map.
- Valid read accesses shall return the current value of the addressed register or register field.
- Valid write accesses shall update the addressed register or register field, subject to write-enable, lock, and shadow-register update rules.
- Accesses to unimplemented, reserved, or otherwise invalid addresses shall produce an error response on the bus interface.
- The module shall support normal reset behavior: all non-shadowed state shall initialize to its reset value on the main reset, and all shadowed register state shall initialize to its reset value on the shadowed reset.

## 3. Interrupt Generation

- The module shall provide one interrupt output per alert class, for a total of four class interrupts.
- For each class, the module shall implement the standard interrupt behavior consisting of:
  - an interrupt enable bit,
  - an interrupt state bit,
  - an interrupt test bit.
- A hardware class-trigger event shall be able to set the corresponding interrupt state bit.
- A software write to the interrupt test bit shall also set the corresponding interrupt state bit.
- Software shall be able to clear the interrupt state bit.
- The interrupt output for a class shall be asserted when the class interrupt state bit is set and the class interrupt enable bit is set.
- After reset, no interrupt output shall be asserted until enabled and set by hardware or software.

## 4. Alert Status and Configuration Mapping

- The module shall maintain sticky cause bits for all external alert sources.
  - A cause bit shall be set when the corresponding enabled alert fires.
  - Once set, the cause bit shall remain set until software clears it.
- The module shall maintain the same sticky cause behavior for all local alert sources.
- The module shall expose the software-programmed alert enable and alert class assignment for each external alert.
- The module shall expose a ping-qualified enable for each external alert.
  - An external alert shall be considered ping-enabled only when its alert enable is set and its alert configuration is locked.
- The module shall expose the software-programmed enable and class assignment for each local alert.
- Local alerts shall not be exposed for ping testing.

## 5. Class Configuration and Clear Protection

- The module shall expose the software-programmed ping timer enable and ping timeout cycle count.
- For each class, the module shall expose:
  - the effective class enable,
  - the autolock configuration,
  - the escalation signal enables,
  - the escalation phase-to-signal mapping,
  - the crashdump trigger phase configuration,
  - the accumulation threshold,
  - the interrupt timeout cycle count,
  - the escalation phase cycle counts,
  - the class clear request.
- The effective class enable for a class shall be true only when all of the following conditions hold:
  - the class master enable is set,
  - at least one escalation signal enable for that class is set.
- The module shall expose a per-class autolock indication based on the class lock configuration.
- The module shall force the class clear write-enable to 0 when:
  - the class has triggered its escalation protocol,
  - the class autolock configuration is set,
  - the class is enabled.
- When the class clear write-enable is forced to 0, software shall not be able to clear that class’s accumulation counter or escalation state.
- When the class clear write-enable is not forced to 0, clearing shall be permitted according to the software-programmed register access rules.
- A software write of 1 to an accepted class clear register shall produce a class clear request.
- The class clear request shall be used to clear the corresponding class accumulation count, escalation count, and escalation state when clearing is allowed.

## 6. Hardware Status to Registers

- The module shall continuously update the software-readable class accumulation count registers from the corresponding hardware accumulator values.
- The module shall continuously update the software-readable class escalation count registers from the corresponding hardware escalation counter values.
- The module shall continuously update the software-readable class escalation state registers from the corresponding hardware escalation protocol state values.
- Software reads of these registers shall observe the current hardware status.

## 7. Crashdump Output

- The module shall provide a crashdump output containing:
  - all external alert cause bits,
  - all local alert cause bits,
  - the current class accumulation counts,
  - the current class escalation counts,
  - the current class escalation state.
- When no crashdump latch is active, the crashdump output shall present the live, current values of these fields.
- The module shall accept a per-class crashdump latch trigger indication.
- If any class latch trigger is asserted and no class latch flag is currently set, the module shall capture the current live crashdump values into a holding register.
- The module shall maintain a per-class latch flag.
  - A latch flag shall be set when the corresponding class latch trigger is asserted.
  - A latch flag shall be cleared when the corresponding class clear request is accepted.
- While any class latch flag is set, the crashdump output shall be held at the captured snapshot value rather than following live status.
- When all class latch flags are cleared, the crashdump output shall return to presenting live status, and a subsequent class latch trigger shall be able to capture a new snapshot.

## 8. Error and Reset Indications

- The module shall provide an indication when a shadowed register storage error is detected.
- The module shall provide an indication when a shadowed register update error is detected.
- The module shall assert a fatal integrity alert output when the bus interface or the register file detects an integrity error.
- These error indications shall be cleared on reset and asserted only while their respective error conditions are present, in accordance with the module’s reset behavior.
